vignette:
He is twenty-six, North American, married, and works as a detective, a job that once made him feel steady in the world. Before the trauma, he describes himself as someone who could read a room quickly, stay calm under pressure, and make sense of other people’s chaos. He met his wife young, and in the beginning he tells the story the way many people do, starting with the good parts: how funny she was, how intensely she loved, how quickly they became inseparable. He says he did not recognize the early warning signs because he was used to seeing violence in other people’s homes, not imagining it could live inside his own.

The first time she hit him, they were arguing late at night in their apartment. He had come home after a long shift, tired and distracted, and she accused him of caring more about work than about her. He remembers trying to keep his voice low, the way he does when interviewing an agitated witness. Then she slapped him hard across the face. He stands very still when he tells this part, as if his body still does not know what to do with the memory. He says his first feeling was not fear but confusion. He had been in fights before, had restrained suspects, had seen men with broken jaws and women with blackened eyes. But this was his wife. He told himself it was stress, that she did not mean it, that if he stayed calm it would not happen again.

It does happen again. Over time the violence becomes woven into ordinary domestic life. An accusation turns into shoving. A slammed door becomes a thrown glass. Once she corners him in the kitchen and strikes him repeatedly in the chest and face while he keeps his hands at his sides, terrified that if he tries to block her, if he leaves a mark, no one will believe his version of events. Another time she wakes him from sleep by yanking the blanket away and hitting him because she thinks he is hiding something from her. He starts to live in anticipation. He listens for the sound of her car in the driveway and feels his stomach drop before he even sees her. He studies the set of her jaw, the rhythm of her footsteps, the volume of cabinet doors, trying to predict whether the night will stay quiet.

What unsettles him most is how his professional identity becomes part of the trap. As a detective, he knows how domestic violence cases are often perceived. He imagines colleagues raising their eyebrows, hears the jokes before they are spoken. He worries that admitting what is happening will make him look weak, or worse, ridiculous. At work he can walk into a tense interview room and keep his breathing even. At home he begins to flinch when his wife moves too quickly. He starts staying late at the station under the pretense of finishing reports. He volunteers for extra follow-up, extra canvassing, any reason not to go home. His work becomes both refuge and strain: he is more alert than ever, but the alertness no longer switches off.

After one particularly violent night, when she throws a heavy object that narrowly misses his head and then punches him while he is trying to get past her to the door, something changes. He leaves the apartment and sits in his car for hours, hands locked around the steering wheel, unable to drive. He notices that he is scanning every mirror, every movement in the parking lot, as if he is the one being pursued. In the days that follow, memories of that night break into his mind without warning. The flash of her arm, the sound of the object hitting the wall, the look on her face seem to arrive whole and immediate. He has trouble sleeping because the moment he starts to drift, his body jerks awake. When he does sleep, he wakes sweaty and disoriented, convinced for a few seconds that she is in the room.

Now, in the present, he lives with a constant sense of threat that he knows does not match his surroundings but cannot shake. Sudden movements make him tense instantly. Raised voices in the bullpen send a shock through his chest. On domestic calls he finds himself going cold and distant or, at other times, unusually activated, jaw tight, wanting the scene secured faster than before. He avoids certain neighborhoods, certain songs, even the cleaning product that smells like their old apartment. He rarely talks to friends because he cannot bear the pity or disbelief he imagines in their faces. With his wife, he is caught between fear, loyalty, shame, and a stubborn hope that keeps collapsing in on itself.

He says the hardest part is that he no longer trusts his own reactions. He used to believe danger was something visible, something he could investigate and name. Now it lives in his body. He startles at small noises, checks locks repeatedly, and sits where he can see the exits in restaurants without consciously deciding to. He feels detached in moments that should be ordinary, as if part of him is always still back in that apartment, listening for footsteps, waiting for the next strike.
